analysis.one_liner: Redirected Central Valley Project water to restore salmon and wildlife habitat and raised below-cost federal farm water prices.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Central Valley Project Reform Act by voice vote on June 18, 1992, but the Senate Energy Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for California's biggest federal dam-and-canal system, the Central Valley Project. It would have dedicated a share of the project's water to restoring salmon, striped bass, and wetland habitat; required farmers who buy federally subsidized water to pay closer to full cost and meter their use; and let water be sold and moved to cities, farms, or environmental uses that value it more. It also included unrelated riders, such as federal payment for defective aqueduct siphons in Arizona.
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial and recreational fishing communities, waterfowl hunters and refuges, urban water users in California, and taxpayers who currently subsidize below-cost farm water would have gained. The bill set a goal of doubling natural salmon production in Central Valley rivers by 2002, guaranteed firm water supplies to federal and state wildlife refuges, and dedicated 100,000 acre-feet of project water to municipal and industrial users through competitive bidding [S3][S4].

how_it_helps.text: Directed the Interior Department to run the Central Valley Project with fish and wildlife restoration as an explicit purpose equal to water delivery and power, and to make project water available for habitat restoration [S3][S4].

Set a program goal of sustaining natural production of salmon and other migratory fish at no less than twice the 1981-1990 average by 2002, with specific fixes for dams, pumps, and diversions that kill fish [S3][S4].
Guaranteed firm water deliveries to Central Valley wildlife refuges and wetlands, reaching full habitat-development supplies within ten years [S3][S4].

Raised farm water prices through tiered pricing, with the top tier at no less than full cost, and required metering of surface water deliveries, reducing the federal subsidy paid by taxpayers [S3][S4].

Authorized voluntary water transfers so water could move to urban users, farms, or environmental purposes, and dedicated 100,000 acre-feet to municipal and industrial buyers at auction, with revenues going to a Restoration Fund [S4].
Allowed citizen lawsuits to force the Interior Department to carry out the bill's mandatory duties [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Central Valley agricultural water contractors would have paid the most: higher tiered water rates, metering costs, responsibility for drainage pollution compliance, and a share of a $15 million annual surcharge on water and power sales to fund restoration. California would have paid 25% of most fish and wildlife mitigation programs, and federal taxpayers would have absorbed large nonreimbursable restoration costs plus unrelated riders like full federal payment for Central Arizona Project siphon repairs [S3][S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm water contractors, power users, California, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Irrigation districts would have faced significantly higher water bills and new compliance costs, which growers could pass on through higher crop prices or reduced planting, a cost bill supporters would have had to acknowledge [S3][S4].

The bill imposed large costs on federal and state budgets, with many restoration programs 37.5% nonreimbursable federal, 25% state-funded, and riders such as nonreimbursable federal payment for defective Central Arizona Project siphons [S4].
The Interior Department submitted unfavorable executive comment on the bill, indicating the administration saw problems with the measure as introduced [S6].
The bill explicitly prohibited authorizing construction of any new water storage facilities, which critics in a growing state could cite as limiting future supply reliability [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade was real: raising subsidized farm water toward full cost and reallocating a share for fish and refuges would have cost agricultural contractors and some public money, but those same revenues and operational changes funded the restoration program and reduced the taxpayer subsidy. The rider-heavy structure, including federal payment for Arizona aqueduct defects unrelated to the Central Valley, was a design weakness that padded the bill with unrelated spending. Overall the environmental restoration and subsidy-reduction benefits appear larger than the costs, though farmers in the project service area would have borne real, concentrated losses.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote on June 18, 1992, the Senate referred it to its Energy and Natural Resources Committee on June 29, and that committee never reported it or brought it to the floor before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: The House Interior and Insular Affairs Committee reported an amended version of the bill on June 16, 1992, after a subcommittee hearing and markup in late May [S6].
The House passed the amended bill by voice vote on June 18, 1992, under a rule allowing one hour of debate [S6].
The Senate received the bill on June 29, 1992, and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where it sat without action for the rest of the 102nd Congress [S6].
The Interior Department had provided unfavorable executive comment on the bill on May 27, 1992 [S6].

The House action record ends on October 8, 1992 with a cross-reference to H.R. 429, a separate water bill in the same Congress, indicating the measure's substance was carried elsewhere in that Congress's final water legislation [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Central Valley agricultural water contractors came out ahead: the bill died before the Senate could act, so below-cost federal farm water contracts, unmeasured deliveries, and current water allocations remained in place for the time being. CVP power users also avoided the new annual restoration surcharge.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm water contractors kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The House passed the bill by voice vote with no recorded roll call, and its 27 cosponsors included 25 Democrats and 2 Republicans, so the record shows bipartisan support in the House but leaves the Senate's position unknown because no vote ever occurred [S5][S6].

industries.industry: Central Valley agricultural water users and irrigated agriculture
industries.note: The bill would have imposed tiered pricing with the top tier at no less than full federal cost, required metering, held contractors responsible for drainage pollution, allowed water transfers away from farms, and authorized buying and retiring subsidized farmland [S3][S4]. This ended part of a long-standing taxpayer subsidy to California irrigation districts, which is why their gain from the bill dying was the public's cost.

industries.industry: Commercial and recreational fishing industry and fishing communities
industries.note: The bill set a goal of doubling natural salmon and other migratory fish production by 2002 and mandated fish screens, passage fixes, and flow standards at project facilities [S3][S4]. Fishing communities and tribes tied to those fisheries would have been the direct beneficiaries.

industries.industry: California municipal and industrial water agencies
industries.note: The bill dedicated 100,000 acre-feet of project water for sale to urban water agencies through competitive bidding and allowed broader voluntary water transfers to cities [S4].

industries.industry: CVP power and water customers (including urban ratepayers)
industries.note: All project power and water sales would have carried an annual surcharge generating $15 million for the Restoration Fund, meaning some of the restoration cost fell on project customers, including municipal users [S4].
The bill required firm water deliveries to national wildlife refuges and state wildlife areas in the Central Valley, phasing up to full habitat-development supplies within ten years [S4].
